title: Canada to Let Eligible Work Permit Holders Study Without a Study Permit
excerpt: IRCC's new temporary measure allows eligible foreign workers to take short-term courses without a separate study permit through December 31, 2027 — a practical boost for professionals upgrading skills while on the job.
body:
• IRCC has introduced a temporary measure allowing eligible foreign workers to study in Canada without a study permit until December 31, 2027.
  • Only courses and programs of six months or less are covered; full-time study still requires a study permit.
  • The policy removes a key restriction: short courses no longer need to be completed within the period of stay originally authorized at entry.
  • No new application is needed — IRCC communicates eligibility to workers directly, who then show their permit to the institution.

The New Measure

Foreign workers in Canada will soon be able to enroll in short-term courses without applying for a separate study permit, under a new temporary public measure from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC). According to immigration consultancy Moving2Canada, the measure is expected to remain in effect until December 31, 2027, and covers programs lasting six months or less.

Under the policy, eligible workers will receive official communication from IRCC confirming that they qualify. From there, the process is simple: they provide a copy of their valid work permit or work authorization letter to the learning institution they plan to attend, according to a legal breakdown published by Stewart McKelvey. There is no separate application to file and no additional fee to pay.

The authorization lasts only as long as the worker's permit is valid, or until the public measure expires — whichever comes first. Workers on maintained status who applied to extend their work permit must have that extension approved to keep studying; a refusal ends the authorization from the date of refusal.

Context & Background

Canada has always allowed temporary residents to take short courses of six months or less without a study permit. But there was a catch in the fine print: the course had to be completed within the period of stay authorized when the person first entered Canada. A worker who entered with a short authorized stay and later received or extended a work permit could find themselves locked out of that provision, even though their legal stay had been extended.

The new temporary policy specifically exempts eligible work permit holders from that requirement, allowing them to complete short-term studies while their work permit remains valid, regardless of the period originally authorized at entry.

This is the second iteration of the idea. A previous measure, in force from June 27, 2023 to June 27, 2026, went further: it lifted the limit on the length of study programs entirely for workers whose permits were issued on or before June 7, 2023, according to Fragomen. The new measure is narrower — capped at six months — but applies to currently eligible workers, making it relevant to today's workforce rather than a legacy cohort.

Impact & Analysis

For Indian professionals in Canada — one of the largest national groups among temporary foreign workers — the change lowers a real barrier to career progression. Short professional courses, licensing exam preparation, and training needed to meet Canadian credential requirements can now be undertaken without a separate IRCC application or the months-long processing that can accompany one.

Stewart McKelvey cautions that the details carry weight. Workers on employer- and occupation-specific permits must continue to honor their permit conditions while studying: if a program would require cutting work hours or relocating in a way that conflicts with the permit, the worker must apply to change those conditions first. Failure to do so risks non-compliance and inadmissibility findings for both worker and employer.

The measure is also explicitly temporary and targeted. It is designed for workers whose primary purpose in Canada is to work, not as a blanket study-permit exemption for temporary residents with a history as foreign workers. And as Fragomen notes, Canadian work experience gained during periods of full-time study does not count toward eligibility for the Canadian Experience Class, nor can students earn Express Entry Comprehensive Ranking System points for it.

Diaspora Angle

Indians form one of the largest cohorts of temporary foreign workers in Canada, concentrated in information technology, healthcare, engineering, and skilled trades — fields where Canadian licensing and credentialing courses are often the gatekeepers to higher pay and career mobility. Removing a layer of immigration paperwork for short professional programs is a practical improvement that reaches exactly the workers who need upskilling most: those already in the country, already working, and trying to move up.

What's Next

IRCC will communicate eligibility to qualifying workers directly, so there is nothing to apply for in advance. Those eyeing longer or full-time programs will still need a standard study permit. Immigration lawyers advise workers to confirm that any course fits within both the six-month cap and the validity of their current work permit before enrolling — and to keep the employer's permit conditions in view for the duration of their studies.
